q: `static TEMPLATE_REGISTRY: &[(&str, &str)] = &[...]` in goose's prompt_template.rs. Which statement is true?
options: It's a borrowed slice of tuples of borrowed string slices, pointing into the binary — zero startup allocation
It's a heap Vec that grows as templates are registered
It's a String-to-String map used as a cache
It returns owned Strings on every access
explanation: Vec is growable and heap-owned; this is a static &[T] slice.
It's not a map; each tuple is (filename, description).
A &str never produces an owned String by itself; you'd have to call to_string().

q: When goose renders `system.md`, the template name is passed as `&str` but the result is a `String`. Why?
options: The name is only a lookup key read briefly; the result is a new value built at runtime that the caller must own
The result must be freed immediately, so it can't be a String
Rust requires all return types to be String
The template name is stored inside the result
explanation: Owned Strings are exactly how freshly built values are returned; an &str return would force borrowing someone else's buffer permanently.
Return types can be &str, String, or anything else — no such rule.
The name is a lookup key that goes out of scope after rendering; it is not stored in the result.

q: What does this print? `let s = String::from("goose agent"); println!("{}", &s[..5]);`
options: "goose"
"goos"
The full string "goose agent"
It does not compile: cannot index a String without &[..] on byte boundaries
explanation: &s[..5] takes the first 5 bytes, which are the five letters "goose".
Slicing &s[..n] yields n bytes, and s itself isn't what's referenced here.
Indexing into a String is disallowed, but a correct byte-bounded slice compiles fine.

q: `let pieces: Vec<&str> = prompt.split(". ").collect();` — what does Rust guarantee here?
options: pieces borrows prompt: no string data is copied, and prompt must outlive pieces
Each piece is duplicated into fresh heap Strings
pieces owns prompt afterwards
split returns one element including the separator
explanation: Vec<&str> holds borrowed slices into prompt; nothing is duplicated.
Borrowing never transfers ownership; prompt remains owned by the original binding.
split's items are the pieces between separators — separators are omitted.

q: Which signature is correct for a function that only reads the text and returns a count?
options: fn word_count(text: &str) -> usize
fn word_count(text: String) -> usize
fn word_count(text: String) -> &str
fn word_count(text: &mut String) -> usize
explanation: Taking String would move/consume the caller's buffer for a read-only operation.
Returning &str would borrow from a parameter the function can't return in this shape.
&mut is unnecessary mutation authority for a read-only count.

q: Fix this compile error: `error[E0308]: mismatched types — expected String, found &str`. `fn greeting() -> String { "hello goose" }`
options: Change the return type to &'static str, since a string literal lives for the whole program's life
Wrap the body in String::new(...)
Add `let mut` before the string literal
Change the literal to a heap type by writing String::"hello goose"
explanation: String::new is an empty constructor and cannot embed a literal.
mut concerns binding mutability, not the literal's type.
There is no String literal syntax; conversion is done via String::from or .to_string().

q: Which of these correctly appends to a string owned by the caller?
options: fn add_marker(s: &mut String) { s.push_str(" END"); }
fn add_marker(s: String) { s.push_str(" END"); }
fn add_marker(s: &str) { s = format!("{s} END"); }
fn add_marker(s: &mut String) -> String { s.push_str(" END"); s }
explanation: Taking String by value mutates a local copy; the caller sees nothing.
&str cannot grow and reassigning the binding locally has no caller effect.
The &mut version already mutates in place; returning s is redundant (though legal-looking, it borrows oddly).
